steps.title: White light and the prism
steps.text: White light contains all the colours. A prism separates them, from violet (around 400 nm) to red (around 700 nm): this is the spectrum. The spectroscope is a small prism placed in an instrument: you look at the light that went through the stone, spread out into its colours.

steps.title: What the stone absorbs
steps.text: When light goes through a coloured stone, the stone keeps some colours: they are missing in the spectrum, and leave dark lines or bands there. What remains is the colour you see. The lines depend on the element that colours the stone: chromium (ruby, emerald), iron (garnets, peridot), manganese, vanadium, copper... The spectrum is therefore a fingerprint of the colour.

steps.title: Reading the spectrum
steps.text: The scale goes from 400 nm to 700 nm: • Violet 400-450 nm • Blue 450-490 nm • Green 490-560 nm • Yellow 560-590 nm • Orange 590-610 nm • Red 610-700 nm Ruby shows a fine line around 694 nm. Fine lines: chromium. Broad bands: iron. In the instrument, move the mouse over the spectrum to read the wavelength.

steps.title: A few spectra
steps.text: • Ruby: chromium lines in the red, a broad yellow-green band. • Emerald: chromium lines in the red (664, 683 nm), nothing in the blue. • Peridot: iron triplet in the blue (451, 470, 494 nm). • Almandine garnet: iron bands, yellow absorbed and two bands in the green. Two green stones, or two red ones, can have very different spectra: the spectroscope sees the cause of the colour.

steps.title: Using the spectroscope
steps.text:
1. Put the stone on the lamp, under the spectroscope.
2. The spectrum appears: look for the dark lines and bands.
3. Move the mouse over them to read their wavelength.
4. Compare with a reference stone, and note what differs.

The instrument does not touch the stone. It needs a coloured, transparent stone: a colourless stone usually gives nothing (except some diamonds, whose spectrum can show lines in the violet).

steps.title: To remember
steps.text: • The spectroscope shows what the stone absorbs, so what colours it, not its name. • Fine lines: most often chromium. Broad bands: iron. • Two stones of the same colour can have two spectra: this is how an imitation is unmasked. • You then need to cross-check with the other measurements.
